content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Great — clean slate. Before I build anything, I want to understand what you're really after, so we make the right thing.

Let me start with the *why* rather than the *what*:

**When this bookmark app is finished and working well, what's different in your day compared to now?** For example — are you drowning in browser bookmarks you can never find again? Saving links across different devices and losing track? Collecting things to read later but never coming back to them? Something else entirely?

And a second thing to help me picture it: **when you save a bookmark, what do you most want to be able to do with it later** — quickly find a specific one, browse by topic, rediscover things you'd forgotten, share a set with someone…?

There are no wrong answers here — just tell me in your own words what's been frustrating or what you're hoping for. Once I understand the goal, I'll show you actual working screens to react to rather than making you read specifications.

My bookmarks are scattered and have become a place where links disappear rather than something I can use. I want one personal collection where I can quickly save a link without much effort, then reliably find it again months later.

When I save something, I’d like the app to fill in useful details from the page automatically, while still letting me adjust the title or description and add a few tags or a note. Later, my priorities are searching by anything I remember, browsing a topic by tag, and keeping a separate “read later” view so unfinished reading doesn’t get mixed into everything else.

content:
That's really clear, thank you — I can picture the problem now. Let me play back what I understand, so we're aligned before I build anything:

**The goal:** One personal, trustworthy collection for your links — so bookmarks stop being a place where things disappear and become something you actually use. Two things matter most:

- **Saving is nearly effortless** — you drop in a link, the app pulls in the useful details itself, and you can lightly adjust the title/description and add tags or a note if you want.
- **Finding it again is reliable, even months later** — through searching by anything you remember, browsing a topic by tag, and a separate "read later" space so unfinished reading stays out of the way of everything else.

Two quick checks to make sure I've got the emphasis right:

1. Is the heart of this really about **trusting that nothing gets lost and you can always find it again** — with effortless saving as the thing that makes you actually keep using it? Or is the effortless capture itself the main prize?

2. When you say "read later" — do you picture a bookmark **starting** in read-later and then graduating into your main collection once you've read it? Or is "read later" just a label/view you flip on and off, with everything living in one collection regardless?

And one thing you haven't mentioned yet: **where do you imagine using this** — mostly at your computer in a browser, on your phone, or both?

Yes, the heart of it is trusting that I can find things again; easy saving is what makes the collection practical enough to keep using.

“Read later” should be a status I can turn on or off while the bookmark remains in the same collection. I’d like a separate view showing only unread items, and marking one as read should remove it from that view without deleting or moving it out of my collection.

I’ll mostly use it in a browser on my computer. Being usable on my phone would be helpful, but the computer experience is the priority.

The prototype now handles the messy cases too — it's live at **http://maker:4001** (refresh). Now that the main flows are settled, I want to walk you through the **boundary and "things go wrong" situations**, since a bookmark tool you can trust has to behave well exactly there. Please try these one at a time:

**1. A page that can't be read automatically.** In the save box, enter `https://broken.example/xyz` and press Save link. Since auto-fill can't get details, you should see an amber notice — *"We couldn't read this page automatically — you can still add it and fill in the details yourself"* — with the title left blank for you to type. Add a title and save it: the point is that a difficult page never blocks you from saving. Does that fallback feel reassuring?

**2. Something that isn't a link.** Type `just some words` (no dot, has spaces) and press Save link. It should gently refuse with *"That doesn't look like a link…"* and not proceed — while a bare address like `example.org/page` (no `https://`) should be accepted normally. Is that the right line to draw?

We've now covered your whole goal, including the rough edges. Here's everything that's settled — in plain terms, no jargon:

**Saving**
- Paste a link and the app fills in the title, description, site icon, and a small preview for you; you review and adjust before it's saved.
- Add tags (with your existing tags suggested so you don't create near-duplicates), an optional note, and flip "Read later" on if you want.
- Saving a link you already have opens that existing bookmark to edit — never a duplicate, even when the address is written slightly differently.
- A page that can't be read automatically still saves — you just fill in the details yourself; and typing something that isn't a link is gently refused.

**Finding again**
- Search across titles, descriptions, notes, tags, and addresses, with a precise language: exact tags with `#`, quoted phrases, and AND/OR/NOT with parentheses — plus a clear warning if a search is malformed.
- Browse a topic either from the tag bar at the top or by clicking a tag on any card; browsing combines with search and both stay visible.
- Sort by newest, oldest, or title (A–Z / Z–A), and your choice is remembered.

**Read later**
- A separate "Read later" view keeps unfinished reading apart; "Mark as read" removes an item from that view but keeps it safely in your collection.

**Throughout**
- Friendly empty states, readable cards even with long text, and a collection that starts empty for real use.

I've recorded your later wishes separately (mobile-friendliness, and control over how many bookmarks show at once) for a future round — they won't be part of this build.

That's 10 settled behaviours covering saving, searching, browsing by tag, sorting, and read-later.

**May I now switch from exploring to actually building this as the real application?** I won't start implementation until you say yes.

Not quite yet. The saving and finding flows are well covered, but “manage” still feels incomplete, so I’m not ready to begin the real build until we settle these areas:

- After saving, I need to be able to edit the address, title, description, tags, and note—not only when a duplicate is detected—and permanently delete a bookmark.
- I need an archive that is clearly different from deletion: archived bookmarks disappear from the normal collection and ordinary searches, have their own view, and can be restored.
- I’d like to select several bookmarks and add or remove tags, mark them read or unread, archive them, or delete them together. The same actions should optionally apply to every bookmark matching the current search, tag, or view.
- Notes should support simple formatting and display that formatting when I view them.
- For links I particularly care about, I want a preserved copy of the page and an option to send it to the Internet Archive. If the link is a PDF, the preserved copy should be the PDF itself.
- I want to save useful combinations of a search and included or excluded tags so I can return to that filtered collection later.
- I need to import and export a standard browser-bookmarks HTML file, keeping details such as titles, tags, and original saved dates.
- Display preferences should include the default sort, how many items are shown, and text size. I’d include the item-count control in this build rather than defer it.
- Selecting a bookmark should open the original page.

Once we’ve explored and agreed on those management and preservation behaviours, I’ll be comfortable authorizing implementation.

The management foundation is in. Please try it and compare the two ways of presenting per-card actions:

**Alternative 1 — actions shown inline.** Open **http://maker:4001/?actions=inline**. Each card shows its buttons directly: the read-later verb button, **✎ Edit**, and **🗑 Delete**.

**Alternative 2 — actions tucked in a "⋯ More" menu.** Open **http://maker:4001/?actions=menu**. The read-later button stays visible, but **Edit** and **Delete** live behind a "⋯ More" menu to keep cards tidy. (This matters because more actions — archive, preserve, etc. — are coming.)

In whichever you're looking at, please walk through these:

1. **Edit any field.** Click **Edit** on a bookmark. The details form opens at the top, now including an **Address** field — change the address, title, description, tags, or note, then **Save changes**. Confirm your edits stick and it updates in place (no duplicate). If you edit the address to one that another bookmark already uses, it should warn you.
2. **Delete permanently.** Click **Delete**. Because this can't be undone, it asks **"Delete this permanently?"** — confirm, and it's gone for good. Does that one-step confirmation feel like enough protection, or too little/too much?
3. **Open by clicking.** Click anywhere on a card (not on a button or tag) — the original page opens in a new tab. Clicking a tag still browses that tag, and clicking a button still does its action.

Three things I decided — tell me if they're right:

- **Which presentation** do you prefer — everything inline, or Edit/Delete behind "⋯ More"?
- **Delete confirmation:** a single inline "are you sure?" — enough, given delete is permanent and there'll also be an archive for the softer case?

A single clear confirmation is enough for permanent deletion, provided it is easy to cancel and archive remains the safer reversible choice. Preventing an edited address from colliding with another saved bookmark is also the right behaviour.
